pos: n. and adj. (one bound by a vow; devoted)
etymology: Latin votus, vowed. Webster (1828): “from Latin votus, from voveo. See Vow.”
biblical_def: A votary is one bound by a vow, and so one devoted to a service or way of life. Webster (1828) defines the noun as “one devoted, consecrated or engaged by a vow or promise; hence more generally, one devoted, given or addicted to some particular service, worship, study or state of life.” He adds: “Every goddess of antiquity had her votaries. Every pursuit or study has now its votaries,” and, sadly, “a great portion of the world are votaries of sensual pleasures.” Every man is a votary of something. Scripture takes vows seriously: “When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it” (Ecc 5:4), and “Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay” (Ecc 5:5). The psalmist says, “I will pay my vows unto the LORD now in the presence of all his people” (Psa 116:14). The believer’s devotion is owed to God alone: “yield yourselves unto God, as those that are alive from the dead” (Rom 6:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): VOTARY, one devoted or engaged by a vow; more generally, one devoted or addicted to some service, worship, study or state of life.
webster_full: VO'TARY, adjective [from Latin votus, from voveo. See Vow.]
Devoted; promised; consecrated by a vow or promise; consequent on a vow.
Votary resolution is made equipollent to custom.

VO'TARY, noun One devoted, consecrated or engaged by a vow or promise; hence more generally, one devoted, given or addicted to some particular service, worship, study or state of life. Every goddess of antiquity had her votaries. Every pursuit or study has now its votaries. One is a votary to mathematics, another is a votary to music, and alas, a great portion of the world are votaries of sensual pleasures.
It was the coldness of the votary not the prayer, which was in fault.
corruption_summary: Votary has lost its root in the vow, and the idea that every man is devoted to some master has faded with it.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster traced the word to the vow and then widened it: a votary of mathematics, of music, of sensual pleasure. His point was moral. Every life is given to something. Modern usage keeps only the mild sense of an enthusiast and forgets that devotion implies a master.
Scripture says the same thing more sharply. Members are yielded either to sin or to God (Rom 6:13). A vow made to God is to be paid (Ecc 5:4), and a heart given to pleasure has made its own vow.

pos: n. (one who lives in solitude for devotion)
etymology: Greek eremites, from eremos, desert. Webster (1828): “Gr. solitary, destitute.”
biblical_def: A hermit is one who withdraws from society to live alone. Webster (1828) defines him as “a person who retires from society and lives in solitude; a recluse; an anchoret,” adding that the word is usually applied to one who lives “disengaged from the cares and interruptions of society, for the purpose of religious contemplation and devotion.” His second sense is “a beadsman; one bound to pray for another.” Scripture commends solitude for prayer. Christ “departed into a solitary place, and there prayed” (Mar 1:35), and “he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed” (Luk 5:16). He taught, “enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6). But He did not ask that His people leave the world: “I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil” (Joh 17:15). His disciples are “the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): HERMIT, a person who retires from society and lives in solitude, usually for religious contemplation; a recluse; a beadsman.
webster_full: HER'MIT, noun [Gr. solitary, destitute.]

1. A person who retires from society and lives in solitude; a recluse; an anchoret. The word is usually applied to a person who lives in solitude, disengaged from the cares and interruptions of society, for the purpose of religious contemplation and devotion.
2. A beadsman; one bound to pray for another.
corruption_summary: The hermit’s life was long praised as a higher holiness, though Christ prayed that His people would stay in the world and be kept from evil.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster describes the hermit’s aim fairly: contemplation and devotion, free of the cares of society. The medieval church went further and ranked the solitary life above the ordinary Christian calling. That ranking has no ground in Scripture, which sends believers into the world as light (Mat 5:14).

The opposite modern error forgets solitude altogether. Christ withdrew to pray (Luk 5:16) and taught secret prayer (Mat 6:6). The pattern is withdrawal for prayer and return to service, not withdrawal for life.

pos: n. (a member of a religious order)
etymology: Latin frater, brother. Webster (1828): “Latin frater. See Brother.”
biblical_def: A friar is a member of one of the religious orders of the Roman church. Webster (1828) defines the word as “an appellation common to the monks of all orders; those who enter religious orders considering themselves as a fraternity or brotherhood.” He names four branches: “Minors, gray friars or Franciscans; 2. Augustines; 3. Dominicans or black friars; 4. White Friars or Carmelites.” In a narrower sense a friar is “a monk who is not a priest; those friars who are in orders being called fathers.” The name means brother, and Scripture gives that name to every believer: “one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8). Christ also said, “call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven” (Mat 23:9). Paul warned against those who are “subject to ordinances” as though still living in the world (Col 2:20), and against teachers “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats” (1Ti 4:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FRIAR, a name common to monks of all orders, who count themselves a brotherhood; Franciscans, Augustines, Dominicans, Carmelites.
webster_full: FRI'AR, noun [Latin frater. See Brother.]

1. An appellation common to the monks of all orders; those who enter religious orders considering themselves as a fraternity or brotherhood. Friars are generally distinguished into four principal branches, viz:1. Minors, gray friars or Franciscans; 2. Augustines; 3. Dominicans or black friars; 4. White Friars or Carmelites.
2. In a restricted sense, a monk who is not a priest; those friars who are in orders being called fathers.
corruption_summary: Friar means brother, but the orders made brotherhood the mark of a separate religious class rather than the common name of all believers.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster notes that friars considered themselves “a fraternity or brotherhood.” In the New Testament that is simply what the church is: “all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8). The orders took a name that belongs to every Christian and made it a title for a vowed few.

The orders also rested on rules of celibacy, poverty and abstinence taken as a higher way. Paul warned against “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats” (1Ti 4:3) as a teaching that departs from the faith.

etymology: Latin rosarium, a rose garden. Webster (1828): “Latin rosarium. See Rose.”
biblical_def: A rosary was first a rose bed. Webster (1828) gives three senses: “a bed of roses, or place where roses grow”; “a chaplet”; and “a string of beads used by Roman catholics, on which they count their prayers.” The practice of counting prayers runs against Christ’s teaching on prayer. “But when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking” (Mat 6:7). Prayer is to the Father in secret (Mat 6:6), and it goes through one Mediator only: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ROSARY, a bed of roses; a chaplet; a string of beads used by Roman Catholics to count their prayers.
webster_full: RO'SARY, noun s as z. [Latin rosarium. See Rose.]
1. A bed of roses, or place where roses grow.
2. A chaplet.
3. A string of beads used by Roman catholics, on which they count their prayers.
corruption_summary: The rosary is often treated as a neutral devotional aid, though it is built on counted repetition and prayers addressed to Mary.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s definition is plain: beads “on which they count their prayers.” The counting is the point. Christ warned that the heathen “think that they shall be heard for their much speaking” (Mat 6:7).

The beads are now sold as jewelry or kept as keepsakes, and the word passes without question. But prayer is not measured by number, and it is not offered through Mary or any saint; there is “one mediator between God and men” (1Ti 2:5).

pos: n. (a book of appointed Scripture readings)
etymology: Latin lectio, a reading, from lego, to read. Webster (1828) enters LEC’TIONARY without an etymology note.
biblical_def: A lectionary is a book of Scripture readings appointed for public worship. Webster (1828) defines it, in the Protestant language of his day, as “the Romish servicebook, containing portions of Scripture.” Lectionaries are now used by many churches. The practice of reading Scripture aloud in worship is older than the church. Ezra’s helpers “read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). In the synagogue Moses was “read in the synagogues every sabbath day” (Act 15:21), and Christ “went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read” (Luk 4:16). Paul charged Timothy, “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13). The question a lectionary raises is not whether to read, but whether the whole counsel of God is read or only chosen portions.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): LECTIONARY, the Romish servicebook, containing portions of Scripture.
webster_full: LEC'TIONARY, noun The Romish servicebook, containing portions of Scripture.
corruption_summary: A lectionary can quietly decide which parts of Scripture a congregation never hears, since it reads appointed portions rather than whole books.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster called the lectionary a book of “portions of Scripture.” Portions are the issue. A cycle of selected readings can pass over hard texts year after year, and a congregation may never hear whole books read in order.

Scripture’s pattern is public reading with the sense given (Neh 8:8) and attendance to reading joined with doctrine (1Ti 4:13). Readings serve the word when they lead into the whole of it, as the reformers’ practice of reading through books (lectio continua) sought to do.

etymology: Latin sermo, speech or discourse. Webster (1828) enters SER’MON without an etymology note.
biblical_def: A sermon is a public discourse grounded on Scripture. Webster (1828) defines it as “a discourse delivered in public by a licensed clergymen for the purpose of religious instruction, and usually grounded on some text or passage of Scripture,” and quotes Dryden: “His preaching much, but more his practice wrought, A living sermon of the truths he taught.” Scripture makes preaching God’s appointed means. “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21). “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14), for “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17). Paul’s charge to Timothy defines the work: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2Ti 4:2). The pattern goes back to Ezra, when they “gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SERMON, a discourse delivered in public by a licensed clergyman for religious instruction, usually grounded on a text of Scripture.
webster_full: SER'MON, noun

1. A discourse delivered in public by a licensed clergymen for the purpose of religious instruction, and usually grounded on some text or passage of Scripture. Sermons are extemporary addresses or written discourses.
His preaching much, but more his practice wrought,
A living sermon of the truths he taught. Dryden.
2. A printed discourse.
SER'MON, verb transitive
1. To discourse as in a sermon [Little Used.]
2. To tutor; to lesson; to teach. [Little Used.]
SER'MON, verb intransitive To compose or deliver a sermon [Little Used.]
corruption_summary: Sermon now often means a talk loosely tied to Scripture, or, in common speech, any tedious moral lecture.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s sermon is “grounded on some text or passage of Scripture.” Many modern talks keep the name but not the ground: a verse is read, then set aside for stories and advice. That is a speech, not a sermon in Webster’s sense.

Ordinary speech also uses “sermon” as a complaint, as in “don’t preach me a sermon.” Scripture does not treat preaching as a nuisance. It is the means God has chosen to save them that believe (1Co 1:21).

pos: n. (a clergyman serving in place of another)
etymology: Latin curatus, one charged with care. Webster (1828): “Latin curator or curatus, from cura, care. See Cure.”
biblical_def: A curate is one who has the care of souls in another’s place. Webster (1828) defines him as “a clergyman in the church of England, who is employed to perform divine service in the place of the incumbent, parson or vicar,” and notes that, “having no fixed estate in the curacy, he may be removed at pleasure.” His second sense is “one employed to perform the duties of another.” The root is cura, care, and the care of souls is the heart of the pastoral office. Peter charged elders to “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). Christ contrasted the shepherd with the hireling, who “fleeth, because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep” (Joh 10:13). The Lord “hath ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel” (1Co 9:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): CURATE, a clergyman employed to perform divine service in place of the incumbent; one employed to perform the duties of another.
webster_full: CURATE, noun [Latin curator or curatus, from cura, care. See Cure.]

1. A clergyman in the church of England, who is employed to perform divine service in the place of the incumbent, parson or vicar. He must be licenced by the bishop or ordinary, and having no fixed estate in the curacy, he may be removed at pleasure. But some curates are perpetual.
2. One employed to perform the duties of another.
corruption_summary: The modern verb curate, to select and arrange, has nearly displaced the noun, and the care of souls in its root is forgotten.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s curate takes his name from cura, care: he has the cure of souls. Today “curate” is mostly a verb for choosing items for a museum or a playlist, and the pastoral sense has faded.

Webster also records the curate’s weak position: no fixed estate, removable at pleasure, doing the work while another held the living. Scripture asks that those who labour be supported (1Co 9:14) and that shepherds care for the flock, not for gain (1Pe 5:2).

etymology: Latin beneficium, a kindness or favor. Webster (1828): “Latin beneficium.”
biblical_def: A benefice is a church office with its income. Webster (1828) notes it means “literally, a benefit, advantage or kindness. But in present usage, an ecclesiastical living; a church endowed with a revenue, for the maintenance of divine service, or the revenue itself.” He explains that “all church preferments are called benefices, except bishoprics, which are called dignities,” and that in the middle ages the word meant a fee or estate in lands before it “became appropriated to church livings.” Scripture allows ministers to be supported: “Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel” (1Co 9:14). But it forbids making the ministry a trade. Elders serve “not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). Paul could say, “I have coveted no man’s silver, or gold, or apparel” (Act 20:33). Micah condemned priests who “teach for hire” (Mic 3:11), and Peter told Simon, “Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money” (Act 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): BENEFICE, literally a benefit; in present usage an ecclesiastical living, a church endowed with a revenue, or the revenue itself.
webster_full: BEN'EFICE, noun [Latin beneficium.]

1. Literally, a benefit, advantage or kindness. But in present usage, an ecclesiastical living; a church endowed with a revenue, for the maintenance of divine service, or the revenue itself. All church preferments are called benefices, except bishoprics, which are called dignities. But ordinarily, the term dignity is applied to bishoprics, deaneries, arch-deaconries, and prebendaries; and benefice to parsonages, vicarages, and donatives.

2. In the middle ages, benefice was used for a fee, or an estate in lands, granted at first for like only, and held ex mero beneficio of the donor. The estate afterwards becoming hereditary, took the appellation of feud, and benefice became appropriated to church livings.
corruption_summary: The benefice turned church offices into property that could be bought, held in plurality, or given as favors, the root of simony.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s history shows the drift: a benefice began as a feudal estate held by favor and became a church living. Once offices carried revenue, they could be sought for the revenue. Simony, the buying of church offices, follows naturally, and Peter’s curse on Simon (Act 8:20) was spoken against exactly that spirit.
Support for ministers is right (1Co 9:14). What Scripture condemns is gain as the motive, teaching “for hire” (Mic 3:11) and serving “for filthy lucre” (1Pe 5:2).
